content: Fluoride mouthrinses have been widely utilized as a preventive measure against dental caries in children and adolescents, both in school-based programs and for individual use at home. This document represents an updated Cochrane review, originally published in 2003, on the effectiveness of fluoride mouthrinses in preventing dental caries in this population. The primary goal of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of fluoride mouthrinses in reducing dental caries among children and adolescents. A secondary objective was to determine whether the effectiveness of fluoride mouthrinses is influenced by factors such as the initial severity of caries, background exposure to fluoride from other sources (e.g., water, salt, toothpaste), or variations in fluoride concentration and frequency of use. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search of multiple electronic databases was conducted, including Cochrane Oral Health's Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, LILACS, BBO, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses, and Web of Science Conference Proceedings. The search spanned publications up to April 22, 2016, and included no restrictions on language or publication date. Additional searches were performed for ongoing trials in the US National Institutes of Health Trials Register and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. Reference lists of articles were reviewed, and selected authors and manufacturers were contacted for further information. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared fluoride mouthrinse with placebo or no treatment in children up to 16 years of age. To be eligible, studies had to last at least one year and assess caries increment as the primary outcome, measured by changes in decayed, missing, and filled tooth surfaces (D(M)FS) in permanent teeth. At least two independent reviewers performed study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment. When necessary, study authors were contacted for additional information. The primary measure of effect was the prevented fraction (PF), which represents the percentage reduction in mean caries increments between treatment and control groups. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted when data could be pooled, and potential sources of heterogeneity were explored using meta-regression analyses. Adverse effects data were also collected from the included trials. A total of 37 trials involving 15,813 children and adolescents were included in the review. All trials evaluated the supervised use of fluoride mouthrinse in schools, with two studies also incorporating home use. Most children used sodium fluoride (NaF) mouthrinse, typically at concentrations of 230 ppm or 900 ppm fluoride, administered daily, weekly, or fortnightly. Of the 37 trials, 28 were assessed as having a high risk of bias, while nine had an unclear risk of bias. Data from 35 trials (15,305 participants) contributed to the meta-analysis of caries increment in permanent tooth surfaces. The pooled prevented fraction (PF) for D(M)FS was 27% (95% confidence interval [CI], 23% to 30%; I² = 42%), based on moderate-quality evidence. Meta-regression analyses revealed no significant association between the prevented fraction and baseline caries severity, background fluoride exposure, rinsing frequency, or fluoride concentration. A funnel plot of the 35 studies showed no evidence of reporting bias. For the 13 trials that provided data on decayed, missing, and filled teeth (D(M)FT), the pooled PF was 23% (95% CI, 18% to 29%; I² = 54%), also based on moderate-quality evidence. Information on adverse effects and treatment acceptability was limited. Three trials reported incomplete data on tooth staining, and one trial provided incomplete information on mucosal irritation or allergic reactions. None of the included trials reported acute adverse symptoms during treatment. The authors concluded that the supervised regular use of fluoride mouthrinse by children and adolescents is associated with a substantial reduction in caries increment in permanent teeth. The evidence supporting this conclusion is of moderate quality. While most of the studies evaluated fluoride mouthrinse use in a school setting, the findings may also apply to other settings where rinsing is supervised or unsupervised, although the magnitude of the preventive effect may vary. Future research should focus on direct comparisons between different fluoride rinse formulations or between fluoride rinses and other preventive strategies. Additionally, future studies should evaluate adverse effects and the acceptability of fluoride mouthrinse regimens.
